Lesson

Prohibition, the Klan, Scopes, and Garvey

🔊 Read aloud: listen to this page
Mr. MagisterYour teacher
Today's Focus

Why did the 1920s produce fierce fights over drink, race, religion, and who counted as a real American?

The same radio programs did not mean the same values. Four stories, Prohibition, the Klan, the Scopes Trial, and Marcus Garvey, show how deep the divisions ran, and the lesson ends by asking which label fits the decade.

Objectives
  1. I will be able to explain why Prohibition failed to win lasting public support and what that failure suggests about law and civic habits
  2. I will be able to describe the Klan, the Scopes Trial, and Marcus Garvey's movement as responses to a changing America
  3. I will be able to evaluate whether the 1920s are better described as a Jazz Age or a culture war
Quick Check-in

If a law banned something many of your neighbors enjoyed, what do you think would happen to it? (No wrong answer. Just check in with yourself.)

The Book
Parts 1 to 3
?
⚡ DECIDE FIRST
Suppose Congress had truly wanted the ban on alcohol to work.
What would it have needed? Decide first and jot down two things that would have helped before you open this.
The lesson points to two. First, enough agents: the government never hired enough to enforce the law across a huge country. Second, support from the people: when many citizens treated the law as a joke, drinkers found speakeasies and bootleggers, and gangs grew rich. Neither was certain. The law had strong supporters among reformers and women's groups, so a different mix of enforcement and public feeling might have given a different result, though nobody can say for sure.
⚡ PUT IT IN ORDER
Put the events of the Tennessee case in order. Tap them one at a time.
    ⚡ ONE THING OR SEVERAL?
    The lesson says many rural and small-town Americans answered change with Prohibition, fundamentalism, and, in some places, the Klan. How much were these one and the same?
    Verdict

    Jazz Age or Culture War?

    My Verdict

    1.Which description fits the 1920s better, a Jazz Age or a culture war, or both about equally? Decide, then defend your verdict with one fact from the book that supports you and one fact that cuts against you.

    The last part says both were real, and asks who was living through each version.

    My Notebook

    A decade rarely fits a single label. Asking who lived through each version gives a truer account.

    Ask Mr. Magister

    Mass Culture and Culture War in the 1920s

    The Culture War

    Part 1

    Drink and the Law

    Chapter 1Four Divisions and the First: Prohibition
    Chapter 1

    Four Divisions and the First: Prohibition

    A country that shares the same radio programs does not necessarily share the same values. In the 1920s, Americans argued fiercely over drink, race, religion, and who counted as a "real American." Four stories show how deep the divisions ran.

    The first is Prohibition. The 18th Amendment was ratified in January 1919 and took effect a year later. It banned making, selling, and carrying alcohol. Its supporters were mostly Protestant reformers and women's groups. They argued that drink wrecked families and wasted wages. A husband could spend a week's pay at the saloon before he reached home on payday, and a wife with no vote had few ways to stop it. The Anti-Saloon League, which cared about one issue and judged politicians only by their votes on it, had been building the movement for decades. An old obstacle had also disappeared. Until the income tax began in 1913, taxes on liquor paid for a large share of the federal government's budget, so a ban would have emptied the Treasury. Now the income tax paid the bills. The war helped them, because many breweries had German names and anti-German feeling was strong. Congress passed the Volstead Act to enforce the amendment, over President Wilson's veto. The act defined an intoxicating drink as anything with more than one-half of one percent alcohol. It still allowed wine for church services and alcohol prescribed by doctors, and the number of prescriptions soared.

    Drinking did fall at first. But the government never hired enough agents to enforce the law across a huge country, with long coastlines and a long border with Canada, where rum-runners brought liquor in by boat and truck. Drinkers found speakeasies, which were illegal bars where jazz bands often played, and bootleggers, who smuggled and sold alcohol. Some bootleg liquor was made badly, and people died from it. Some of the danger came from the government itself. Alcohol made for factories was ordered mixed with poisons so that no one would drink it, and when bootleggers cleaned it up and sold it anyway, many drinkers died. Enforcers did try. In New York, two agents named Izzy Einstein and Moe Smith became famous for showing up at speakeasies in disguises, from a fisherman to a gravedigger, and they made several thousand arrests before they were dismissed in 1925. Cocktails became popular partly because the mixers hid the harsh taste. Criminal gangs grew rich. In Chicago, Al Capone ran a bootlegging empire and had rivals killed. In 1929, his men murdered seven rival gang members in the St. Valentine's Day Massacre. Capone was finally sent to prison in 1931, not for the killings, but for not paying taxes on his income. The lesson was a classical one. A law needs the support of the people it governs, and when many citizens treat a law as a joke, respect for all law suffers. A federal commission named by President Hoover and led by George Wickersham reported in 1931 that the law was widely broken and badly enforced, yet most of its members still did not want it repealed. The country ended Prohibition in 1933 with the 21st Amendment, the only time one amendment has repealed another.

    Part 2

    Hate and Belief

    Chapter 2The Klan Rises and Falls
    Chapter 3The Trial in Dayton
    Chapter 2

    The Klan Rises and Falls

    The second story is darker. The Ku Klux Klan was revived in 1915 at Stone Mountain, Georgia. A new film that year, The Birth of a Nation, had praised the old Klan of the Reconstruction years, and a man named William Simmons gathered a few dozen men on the mountain one night to start a new one. In the 1920s it spread far beyond the South, into Indiana, Ohio, Oregon, and other states. It claimed several million members at its peak. It attacked Black Americans, Catholics, Jews, and immigrants, and its members used whippings, beatings, and murder. Many Klan groups also presented themselves as ordinary civic clubs, with parades, picnics, and talk of patriotism. Its leaders earned money by selling memberships and robes. A new member paid a ten-dollar fee, and the recruiter who signed him up kept a share, so recruiting became a business. The Klan also gave its officers grand titles. The national leader was called the Imperial Wizard, a state leader a Grand Dragon, and the head of a local group an Exalted Cyclops.

    In some states, the Klan won real power. In Indiana, where perhaps a quarter of a million men joined, it became a force in state politics. In Oregon, it helped pass a law that would have required every child to attend public school, a law aimed at Catholic schools. The Supreme Court struck it down in 1925. In August of that year, tens of thousands of Klan members in white robes marched down Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington. The Klan collapsed in the late 1920s after scandals, including the 1925 murder conviction of an Indiana Klan leader named D. C. Stephenson, who held the title of Grand Dragon. Stephenson had boasted that he was the law in Indiana. His conviction showed that the man at the top was a criminal, and members left by the thousands. Judged by the republican tradition, the Klan was a clear failure of civic culture. It claimed to protect the community, but it set citizen against citizen and put violence above law.

    Chapter 3

    The Trial in Dayton

    The third story took place in a small Tennessee town. Fundamentalists were Protestants who held that the Bible must be read literally. Many of them were alarmed that public high schools were teaching Darwin's theory of evolution. Their side argued that parents and taxpayers had the right to decide what their own public schools taught. Bryan, their best-known champion, also feared that the idea of the survival of the fittest could be used to excuse war and ruthless competition. In 1925, Tennessee passed a law that banned teaching that humans had descended from lower animals. The American Civil Liberties Union offered to defend any teacher who would test the law. Business leaders in Dayton, Tennessee, hoping for publicity, persuaded a young teacher named John Scopes to be the defendant. They met in a drugstore on Main Street to plan it. Scopes was a twenty-four-year-old science teacher and football coach, and he later said he was not sure he had ever actually taught evolution.

    The Scopes Trial drew the nation's attention. William Jennings Bryan, a three-time candidate for president, helped the prosecution. Clarence Darrow, one of the best-known lawyers in America, defended Scopes. Darrow had become famous the year before by saving two wealthy teenagers, Leopold and Loeb, from the death penalty for a murder in Chicago. Radio carried the trial across the country. Dayton filled with reporters, preachers, and street vendors, and in the July heat the court moved outside to the courthouse lawn for a day. At one point, Darrow called Bryan to the stand as an expert on the Bible, and Bryan struggled under his questions. The judge had ruled that Darrow could not call scientists to speak for evolution, so Darrow called the other side's champion instead. Then Darrow did something odd. He asked the jury to find his own client guilty. That let the case move to a higher court, and it also kept Bryan, who had prepared a closing speech, from ever giving it. The jury took only minutes to convict Scopes, and he was fined one hundred dollars. The Tennessee Supreme Court later threw out the conviction on a technicality. The jury, it said, and not the judge, should have set the fine. Bryan died five days after the trial. Reporters from the big cities mocked the townspeople. H. L. Mencken, a sharp-tongued writer for a Baltimore newspaper, sent home some of the sharpest stories. Many rural Americans felt mocked in turn. The law stayed on the books for more than forty years.

    Part 3

    Pride and the Ballot

    Chapter 4Marcus Garvey and the UNIA
    Chapter 5A Country Split in Two
    Chapter 6The Real 1920s
    Chapter 4

    Marcus Garvey and the UNIA

    The fourth story is about a movement of pride among Black Americans. Marcus Garvey came to New York from Jamaica in 1916. He founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association, which preached pride in African heritage, Black-owned businesses, and self-reliance. In August 1920, thousands of his followers paraded through Harlem in uniforms and filled Madison Square Garden. Garvey claimed millions of members, and historians think the true number was far smaller, but still very large. The association ran its own newspaper, the Negro World, and a string of Black-owned small businesses, including grocery stores and a laundry. Some of his followers also hoped to build a new life in Africa, and Garvey talked with Liberia about land for a settlement, though Liberia's government backed away in 1924. The association also adopted a flag of red, black, and green, which later became a symbol of Black pride around the world.

    Garvey started a shipping company called the Black Star Line and sold stock to thousands of Black buyers. Shares sold for five dollars each, so even poor families could own a piece of a Black-owned fleet. The ships were old and the business failed. In 1923, Garvey was convicted of mail fraud. He went to prison in 1925. President Coolidge later cut his sentence short, and Garvey was deported in 1927. Black leaders such as W. E. B. Du Bois, who worked for full citizenship and equal rights inside the United States, criticized Garvey sharply. But Garvey's message of dignity reached many people who felt shut out of the national story. The movement shows that the Harlem Renaissance and the Jazz Age were not the only things happening in Black America. Some Black Americans saw hope in the nation's promises, and some had stopped believing in them.

    Chapter 5

    A Country Split in Two

    These four stories point to a split in the country. The 1920 census showed that, for the first time, most Americans lived in towns and cities instead of on farms and in villages. Cities were crowded and full of immigrants. They were home to jazz, speakeasies, and new ideas about manners and religion. Many rural and small-town Americans felt that their way of life was being pushed aside. They answered with Prohibition, with fundamentalism, and, in some places, with the Klan. These were not the same thing, and it would be unfair to treat them as one. Prohibition, for example, had many sincere and decent supporters. But all of them were ways of asking who owned the country's future.

    Chapter 6

    The Real 1920s

    The presidential election of 1928 put the split on the ballot. The Democratic candidate, Governor Al Smith of New York, was the son of immigrants, a Catholic, a product of city politics, and an open opponent of Prohibition. Many city voters admired him. Many rural Protestants distrusted him, and some attacked him because of his faith. Whispering campaigns and some preachers warned that a Catholic president would take orders from the Pope. Herbert Hoover, a Protestant and a supporter of the "noble experiment" of Prohibition, won in a landslide. He took 444 electoral votes to Smith's 87, and he even carried several Southern states that had rarely voted Republican since Reconstruction. Smith lost, but he also pulled millions of new voters from the cities into the Democratic Party, a change that would matter in the next decade. He carried the country's twelve largest cities. One more result of that November mattered more than it seemed. Franklin Roosevelt, who had placed Smith's name in nomination at the convention, narrowly won the governorship of New York in the same election in which Smith lost the state.

    So which was the real 1920s? The Jazz Age was real. The mass culture you studied in the last lesson was real. So was the culture war. Historians often try to fit a decade into a single label, but a decade rarely fits. A better approach is to ask who was living through each version. A young clerk in New York, a farm family in Tennessee, and a Black family in Harlem could all have lived the 1920s very differently, and all of them would have been telling the truth. What held the country together through these fights was the Constitution's framework of ordinary law. How well that framework would hold up under a far greater strain is the subject of the next two weeks.
